e.etymology: A spelling of Caden, which rose in the early 2000s alongside the similar-sounding Aidan, Braden, Hayden and Jadon.
From Hebrew Gid'on, feller or hewer. In the Book of Judges Gideon defeats the Midianites with only 300 men; the Puritans brought the name into English use.

assoc.t: Gideon Bibles left in hotel rooms

e.meaning: of a king or queen, regal
e.etymology: Mostly the English word royal, from Old French roial and Latin regalis, kingly. It is also an English surname from places such as Ryal and Ryhill, named for a hill where rye grew.
From the Welsh surname ab Owain, son of Owen. It has been used as a first name in the US mainly since the 2000s.

e.meaning: the giant hunter of Greek myth, set among the stars
e.etymology: The name of a giant hunter in Greek myth who was placed in the sky as a constellation. The origin of the Greek name itself is unknown.
A modern spelling of Adeline, a French pet form of Adele, from the Germanic word adal, noble. The -lyn ending follows names such as Madelyn and Evelyn.
A spelling of Eric, from Old Norse Eirikr, usually explained as ei, ever, plus rikr, ruler. This spelling is especially common in Spanish-speaking families.
From an English surname meaning son of Coll, a medieval short form of Nicholas. As a first name it is a 21st-century arrival that fits with Colton and Carson.
A modern name built from Kay and the ending -la. It spread fast in the 1980s after the character Kayla Brady appeared on the soap opera Days of Our Lives.

e.meaning: short form of Teresa, perhaps harvester
e.etymology: A contraction of Teresa, a name first recorded in Spain whose source is unclear; it is often linked to Greek therizo, to harvest.
namesakes: Tessa Thompson (actress, Creed and Thor: Ragnarok)

e.etymology: A recent American spelling of Zaire, the former name of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and of the Congo River, from a Kongo word for river.
A name with several possible sources: the Russian city of Samara on the Volga, the Iraqi city of Samarra, and samara, the winged seed of a maple. Its meaning as a given name is not settled.
namesakes: Samara Weaving (Australian actress, Ready or Not)

assoc.t: ghost girl who climbs out of the TV in The Ring
city on the Volga River in Russia
samara, the winged helicopter seed of a maple

e.note: Samara is the ghost girl of the 2002 horror film The Ring; horror fans will make the link.

e.etymology: The Spanish and Romanian form of Christian, from Latin Christianus, follower of Christ. In the US it is used mostly by Hispanic families.
The Spanish form of Joachim, from Hebrew Yehoyaqim, raised up by Yahweh. By tradition Saint Joachim was the father of the Virgin Mary.
Invented by Jonathan Swift in the early 1700s for his friend Esther Vanhomrigh, joining Van from her surname to Essa, a pet form of Esther. It was later given to a genus of butterflies.
The Spanish and Portuguese form of Lionel, a medieval pet form of Leon, from Latin leo, lion.
From the English word for a thorny bush such as the wild rose, Middle English brere. In the Grimm fairy tale Sleeping Beauty is called Briar Rose.
namesakes: Briar Rose (Sleeping Beauty's name in the fairy tale and the Disney film)

assoc.t: Briar Rose, the Sleeping Beauty of fairy tale and Disney

e.etymology: A spelling of Evelyn with the -lynn ending. Evelyn began as an English surname from the Norman woman's name Aveline, whose meaning is uncertain.

assoc.t: Evelynn, a champion in the game League of Legends

e.meaning: dew of the sea (the herb); also Rose plus Mary
e.etymology: A blend of Rose and Mary first recorded in the 1700s, later also taken from the herb rosemary, Latin ros marinus, dew of the sea.
namesakes: Rosemary Kennedy (sister of John F. Kennedy)

e.etymology: An Italian pet form of Angela, from Greek angelos, messenger.
namesakes: Angelina Ballerina (dancing mouse of children's books and TV)

e.etymology: From Latin Joanna and Greek Ioanna, the feminine of the Hebrew name Yochanan, God is gracious, which also gave John. In Luke's Gospel Joanna is one of the women who follow Jesus.
namesakes: Joanna Gaines (designer and host of Fixer Upper)

e.etymology: The Spanish, Portuguese and Central European feminine of Gabriel, from Hebrew Gavri'el, God is my strength, the name of the archangel.
The Spanish and Portuguese form of Ezekiel, from Hebrew Yechezqel, God strengthens, the name of the Old Testament prophet.
The Spanish and Portuguese short form of Emanuel, from Hebrew Immanu'el, God is with us. It has been in use in Spain and Portugal since the Middle Ages.
From Hebrew Azaryah, Yahweh has helped, borne by many men in the Old Testament, among them the companion of Daniel also known as Abednego. In the US it is now given to both boys and girls.
From an English surname for someone who lived by a ford, Old English waed. It has been a steady American first name since the 1800s.
namesakes: Wade Boggs (Hall of Fame third baseman)

assoc.t: Roe v. Wade, the 1973 abortion ruling

e.etymology: The Latin Bible's form of Hebrew Rivqah, probably from a root meaning to tie or bind and often glossed as captivating. Rebecca is the wife of Isaac and mother of Jacob and Esau.
namesakes: Rebecca (wife of Isaac in the Book of Genesis)
Rebecca Ferguson (actress, Dune and Mission: Impossible)

assoc.t: Rebecca, Daphne du Maurier's novel and Hitchcock's film

e.etymology: From an English surname taken from villages named Bradley, Old English brad, broad, plus leah, wood or clearing.

assoc.t: Bradley Fighting Vehicle of the US Army

e.etymology: From Arabic khalil, close friend. In Islamic tradition Abraham is called Khalil Allah, the friend of God.
namesakes: Kahlil Gibran (poet, author of The Prophet)

e.etymology: A spelling of Arabic Layla, related to layl, night, known from the old love story of Layla and Majnun. A separate Laila, of unclear origin, has been used in Finland and Scandinavia since the 1800s.
namesakes: Laila Ali (boxing champion, daughter of Muhammad Ali)

e.etymology: From two Arabic names written alike in English: Amina, trustworthy, the feminine of Amin, and Aminah, safe, the name of the mother of the Prophet Muhammad.
Borrowed into English in the 1800s from more than one source: Russian Nina, the name of a 4th-century saint of Georgia, and an Italian short form of names such as Annina and Giovannina.
namesakes: Nina Simone (singer and civil rights voice)

assoc.t: the Niña, one of Columbus's three ships

e.note: Close to Spanish niña, little girl, so Spanish speakers may hear the word.
